one_liner: Eigen-based C++ kd-tree for exact (or epsilon-approximate) k-NN in low dimensions; the README claims 5-20% faster than ANN.
what_it_does: Answers k-nearest-neighbour queries over a point cloud stored as a column-major Eigen matrix (one point per column), for float or double. Each query returns the indices and squared distances of the k nearest points. A factory (NNSearchF::createKDTreeLinearHeap, createKDTreeTreeHeap, createBruteForce) returns a polymorphic search object, and knn() takes either one query vector or a matrix of queries. Options include an epsilon for approximate search, a maximum radius (one value, or one per query) and flags for self-match and result sorting. It is not a drop-in for ANN: the API is Eigen-based and has no BD-tree and no non-Euclidean metrics.
how_it_is_fast: It is ANN's sliding-midpoint kd-tree (ANN_KD_SL_MIDPT) with a more compact memory layout. Points sit in buckets at the leaves (default bucketSize 8). Nodes live in one contiguous array; the left child is implicitly the next node, and the split dimension and right-child index share one packed uint32. Cell bounds are not stored, and the search tracks incremental offsets as in ANN's paper. The authors credit the roughly 5-fold smaller memory footprint for the speed, since the search is memory-bound. Two heap variants exist: a linear vector heap for small k (up to about 30) and an STL tree heap for larger k. The matrix knn() overload runs queries in parallel with OpenMP, which is on by default in CMake.
when_to_use: ICP or point-cloud registration in 2D or 3D on CPU, especially if your code already uses Eigen matrices. The ICP paper the README cites evaluates exactly this use, and the CHANGELOG muted Ubuntu jammy 'until libpointmatcher build pass on jammy', so the two projects are built together.
Many queries at once: pass them as one matrix so the size checks run once and OpenMP spreads the queries across threads.
Exact or bounded-error kNN with a per-query maximum radius to prune the search, for example outlier rejection in registration.
Replacing ANN in old C++ code with a reentrant, BSD-licensed library templated on scalar type (float or double).
Projects that also want Python (pynabo, via Boost.Python) or a pure-Rust port (nabo-rs) of the same algorithm.
when_not_to_use: High-dimensional data (descriptors, embeddings): it is built for low dimensions and offers only Euclidean distance, with no approximate high-dimensional index. Use FLANN or an ANN-graph library.
Header-only or zero-dependency builds: it is a compiled CMake library that needs Eigen, plus Boost for the Python bindings. nanoflann is header-only.
Dynamic point sets: the tree is built once over the given cloud, with no insert or delete. Pkd-tree supports batch updates.
Fixed-radius searches that return every point within r: knn() returns at most k results, and the radius only prunes.
New projects on recent toolchains: CI tests only Ubuntu 18.04 and 20.04, the project builds as C++11, and Eigen 5 compatibility (#147) and MSVC build failures (#124, #113) are open issues.

integration.dependencies: Eigen 2 or 3 (header-only); optional Boost.Python for pynabo; optional OpenMP (on by default, links gomp under GCC); optional OpenCL code paths are disabled by default ('not up-to-date with API')
integration.platforms: x86 and arm64 on Ubuntu 18.04 and 20.04 (tested in CI); macOS and Windows 'reportedly' work, per the README
integration.thread_safety: The FAQ says it is reentrant, unlike ANN. Each knn() call keeps its own heap, and the matrix overload is OpenMP-parallel internally. Concurrent knn() calls on one const object look safe from the source, but the README does not state this.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same sliding-midpoint kd-tree and bucket size as ANN, but an Eigen-matrix API, Euclidean distance only and no BD-tree, so calling code must be rewritten

gotchas: The point matrix is held by reference: 'M must stay alive throughout the use of libnabo, otherwise the results of knn are undefined.' create() returns a raw owning pointer you must delete.

Self-matches are excluded by default. The check is squared distance > numeric_limits<T>::epsilon() (about 1.2e-7 for float), so exact duplicate points and any neighbour closer than about 3.5e-4 units in float are silently dropped unless you pass ALLOW_SELF_MATCH.

Results are unsorted unless SORT_RESULTS is set. Missing neighbours (radius limit) come back as InvalidIndex and infinite distance. Asking for k >= cloud size (k > size - 1 without self-match) throws std::runtime_error.

The node index shares a 32-bit field with the split dimension, so the constructor throws if cols/(bucketSize/2) could exceed 2^(32 - dimBits) - 1 nodes, and Index is a 32-bit int. Very large or higher-dimensional clouds need a larger bucketSize.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libnabo over nanoflann, picoflann or PicoTree when you already store points as Eigen matrices in an ICP stack and want batched, OpenMP-parallel exact kNN with per-query radius limits. nanoflann (header-only, no Eigen requirement) and PicoTree (which publishes numbers against nanoflann) are easier to adopt and better documented on speed. SPRK-tree's harness benchmarks nabo, but no numbers were seen.
verified_claims_summary: The only speed claim is first-party: the README and the doxygen FAQ say libnabo is 'about 5% to 20% faster than ANN (both -O3 -NDEBUG), probably due to the smaller memory footprint', with no CPU, dataset or table. tests/knnbench.cpp compares against ANN only when ANN is installed, and publishes nothing. In its current form it times libnabo's matrix knn(), OpenMP-parallel when OpenMP is found, against ANN queried one point at a time on one thread, so today's 'make test' numbers would not be a like-for-like comparison. The JOSER 2012 paper (co-authored by the libnabo author) that should hold the measurements was unreachable here (stephane.magnenat.net and uni-wuerzburg.de are egress-blocked); search snippets confirm only that it compares 3DTK, ANN, CGAL, FLANN, libnabo, SpatialIndex and STANN for ICP.
